name: Leucine
lead: Leucine is an essential branched-chain amino acid (BCAA): the human body cannot make it, so it must come from dietary protein such as meat, dairy, soy and legumes [1]. Along with isoleucine and valine it is one of the three BCAAs, and it is sold both as a stand-alone powder and as an ingredient in BCAA, essential amino acid and pre- or intra-workout products.

In muscle-building communities leucine is discussed as the amino acid that most directly switches on muscle protein synthesis, through activation of the mTOR signalling pathway [1][13]. Laboratory work has identified several intracellular leucine sensors, including Sestrin2 and SAR1B, that feed into mTORC1 [13][14].

Human trials show that protein supplementation in general modestly increases gains in lean mass and strength during resistance training [3]. Evidence that adding isolated leucine to an already adequate protein intake produces further gains in healthy trainees is limited; most clinical work on leucine-enriched products has been done in older adults with sarcopenia, with mixed results [5][7].

paras: Leucine is taken mainly by people who lift weights or who want to preserve lean mass, either as free-form L-leucine or inside whey protein, BCAA blends and essential amino acid products. Because whey and casein are rich in leucine, many forum discussions treat dietary protein quality as a proxy for leucine content, and some posters argue that soy protein is less effective than whey in part because of its lower leucine content [31].
Clinically, leucine-enriched formulas are studied as nutritional support in sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss), frailty and muscle disuse [7][8][9][11].

A 2018 meta-analysis of 49 randomised trials (1,863 participants) found that protein supplementation during at least six weeks of resistance training produced small average increases in strength, fat-free mass and muscle cross-sectional area, with the effect on fat-free mass smaller with increasing age and larger in resistance-trained people [3]. This analysis concerns total protein, not leucine in isolation.

A 12-week randomised trial in men and women compared soy and whey protein supplements that were matched for leucine content and reported no significant differences in muscle growth or strength [10]. Researchers and forum participants cite this kind of result in discussions of whether leucine content explains differences between protein sources.

The Wikipedia article notes that results of studies on supplemental leucine are conflicting and that long-term supplementation has not been shown to raise muscle mass or strength in healthy elderly men [1].

Leucine is a normal dietary component. In decompensated maple syrup urine disease, a genetic disorder of branched-chain amino acid metabolism, leucine accumulation causes delirium and neurological compromise and can be life-threatening [1].

High leucine intake has been proposed to worsen pellagra in people with low niacin status, because it interferes with conversion of tryptophan to niacin, and intakes above about 500 mg/kg/day have been associated with raised blood ammonia; an unofficial upper level of about 35 g/day for healthy men under acute conditions has been suggested [1].

Elevated circulating BCAAs, including leucine, are associated with insulin resistance and with future type 2 diabetes risk in observational metabolomic studies [6]. Whether this reflects cause, effect or a marker of other metabolic changes is not established by those studies. Reports from users and gastrointestinal complaints at high doses are discussed informally; one T Nation poster notes that straight leucine powder is difficult to dissolve [28].

Leucine directly stimulates myofibrillar protein synthesis by activating mTOR, a kinase that regulates protein synthesis and cell growth. The activation involves Rag GTPases, leucyl-tRNA synthetase and the sensor Sestrin2, and possibly other mechanisms [1]. Sestrin2 was described in 2016 as a leucine sensor for the mTORC1 pathway [13], and in 2021 SAR1B was reported as another leucine-sensing protein [14].
Reviews of human muscle physiology describe how nutrients and muscle contraction both regulate protein synthesis and mTORC1 signalling [15].

Most dietary leucine is handled in the liver, fat and muscle. Around 60% is metabolised within several hours, about 40% ends up as acetyl-CoA, and roughly 5% (range 2 to 10%) is converted to beta-hydroxy beta-methylbutyrate (HMB), a minor metabolite also sold as a supplement [1]. Leucine is one of only two exclusively ketogenic amino acids [1].

Leucine is an aliphatic alpha-amino acid with an isobutyl side chain (formula C6H13NO2) [1][2]. The name derives from the Greek for 'white'. According to Grokipedia, it was first isolated from cheese in 1819 by Joseph Louis Proust and from wool and muscle in 1820 by Henri Braconnot [2]; this account has not been checked against a primary source.

Trials of leucine in humans fall into a few groups. In older adults with sarcopenia, a meta-analysis of three studies (637 patients) of whey protein, leucine and vitamin D combinations found no significant difference in grip strength or short physical performance battery scores overall, but appendicular muscle mass improved; with a concurrent exercise programme, grip strength and performance scores improved [5].

The PROVIDE trial, a multicentre double-blind randomised study, tested a vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey supplement in older adults with sarcopenia [7]. A two-month randomised trial of a food containing 2.5 g leucine, omega-3 fatty acids and a probiotic strain in older people with sarcopenia also reported on lean mass, performance and inflammation [8]. A de-training follow-up trial examined leucine-enriched whey with resistance training over 24 weeks [9], and further randomised trials tested multi-component supplements for frailty and for rehabilitation in sarcopenia [11][12]. Because these products combine leucine with other ingredients, they do not isolate leucine's own effect.
An umbrella review of nutritional interventions in people aged 65 and over assessed supplementation across several muscle outcomes [4].

Registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov include studies of leucine dose and muscle maintenance during weight loss (NCT07583875), leucine to offset disuse atrophy (NCT03762278), leucine in older-age anabolic responses (NCT06567665), leucine requirements, and leucine in Diamond Blackfan anemia [16][17][18][19][20].

timeline.event: Leucine is first isolated from cheese by Joseph Louis Proust, according to Grokipedia [2].
Henri Braconnot obtains it from hydrolysed wool and muscle [2].
The US Food and Nutrition Board sets an RDA for essential amino acids, including leucine [1].
Sestrin2 is reported as a leucine sensor for mTORC1 [13].
A 49-study meta-analysis quantifies the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training gains [3].
SAR1B is reported as a leucine sensor regulating mTORC1 [14].

lore.intro: On T Nation, leucine is discussed as the 'key amino acid for muscle protein synthesis' and as a component of pre-workout formulas, with debate about whether stand-alone leucine or BCAAs add anything beyond whole protein [24][28][29].

claims.claim: Leucine 'turns on' mTOR and is the key trigger for muscle growth
claims.believers: Forum posts and articles describe leucine as the amino acid that activates mTOR and maintains or increases muscle, and recommend leucine-rich whey and casein for this reason [24][29].
claims.experts: Laboratory studies confirm leucine-sensing pathways that feed mTORC1 [13][14], and the mechanism is described in reference works [1]. Whether supplementing extra leucine raises long-term muscle gain in well-fed healthy people is not established [1].

claims.claim: Soy protein is inferior to whey because of lower leucine content
claims.believers: A T Nation thread on soy notes that soy was inferior to whey in a cited study and attributes this to differences in quality, digestibility and leucine content [31].
claims.experts: A 12-week trial that matched soy and whey supplements for leucine found no significant differences in muscle growth or strength [10].

claims.claim: Adding leucine to a pre- or post-workout drink offers extra benefit
claims.believers: Users of a commercial workout formula that contains 5 g of leucine ask or report on what leucine and malic acid add, and some describe the product as working well [26][27].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested that specific formula; trials of leucine-enriched products have largely been in older adults with sarcopenia and combine leucine with other nutrients [5][7].

claims.claim: Leucine alone, not BCAA blends, is what matters (or BCAAs are not needed if protein is adequate)
claims.believers: One poster tells others to drop BCAAs and rely on whole animal proteins and eggs, saying protein itself drives insulin and meeting daily protein matters more than timing [30].
claims.experts: The 2018 meta-analysis supports a benefit of total protein supplementation during resistance training [3]; direct comparisons of leucine against BCAA products in trained people are not reported in the cited literature.
